shell.title: Light overhead, none underfoot
shell.mini: After sunset the air overhead stays sunlit while the ground is in shadow. On a globe, the shadow's ceiling is set by the radius: 35 km when the Sun is 6° down, 142 km at 12°, 328 km at 18°. On a plane nothing can cast that shadow.
shell.text: Long after sunset the sky stays bright while the ground is dark. A lit sky over unlit ground needs an edge, and an edge needs a shadow cast by a body big and round enough. On a globe, when the Sun is θ below your horizon, the last ray grazing the Earth passes over your head at a height h = R(sec θ − 1): 35 km at 6°, 142 km at 12° and 328 km at 18°, the thresholds of civil, nautical and astronomical twilight [1]. Below that height you are in the planet's shadow; above it the air is in sunlight and scatters some down to you. The drawing is at true scale, which is why the lit shell is so thin. It makes no claim about how bright the scattering is [2], only that a boundary exists and that R sets its height. On a plane the Sun is above the ground at every hour: nothing can be in shade while the air above it is lit.
shell.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a twilight sky that is not brighter overhead than the ground below, or an Earth's shadow that does not rise with the Sun's depression.
ceiling.title: How high the Earth's shadow reaches
ceiling.mini: The last sunbeam that grazes the Earth at the day-night line passes over an observer further round at a height set by the radius and by how far the Sun is below the horizon: h = R(sec θ − 1).
ceiling.text: When the Sun is θ below your horizon, the last ray that grazes the Earth's surface at the day-night line passes over your head at a height h. Below h you are in the planet's shadow; above it the air is still in full sunlight. The single line h = R(sec θ − 1) is the whole geometry of twilight, and it contains R, so twilight is a measurement of the radius rather than merely a consequence of it. The drawing is schematic.
ceiling.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a twilight whose sunlit layer does not rise as the Sun sinks.
lamp.title: A lamp over a plane
lamp.mini: Put a Sun of diameter D at height H over an infinite plane. An observer at distance d receives less light and sees a smaller Sun. Both follow from one slant distance, whatever H, D and brightness are.
lamp.text: The flat model taken seriously and given its best case: a Sun of diameter D at height H above an infinite plane, as small and close as it likes, its light falling off as the inverse square of distance, the correct law for a compact source and the law flat-Earth accounts appeal to when they explain sunset as the Sun becoming distant and dim. An observer at ground distance d from the point under it is at slant range √(H² + d²). The light on level ground and the Sun's apparent size both follow from that one distance, for any H, any D and any brightness. The drawing is schematic.
lamp.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: sunset light that dims without the Sun's disc shrinking.
cancel.title: On a plane, dark means small
cancel.mini: Divide by noon and every free parameter cancels: on a plane, the ground can only get darker to the exact extent the Sun gets smaller. Night is 100 million times darker than noon, so the Sun would have to shrink 464-fold. It does not.
cancel.text: Divide the light on the ground and the Sun's apparent size by their values at noon and every free parameter cancels: the height, the diameter and the brightness of the Sun all disappear. What is left links two things a phone can measure: on a plane, the ground can only get darker to the exact extent the Sun gets smaller, as the cube of its apparent size. Measured, night is about 100 million times darker than noon [1]. The flat Sun would therefore have to shrink 464-fold, from 32′ to 4″, crossing the sky from a disc to a star. Tune the height to make night dark enough and the Sun sits 43 km up; keep the disc its real size and midnight is only 70 times darker than noon. The drawing is schematic.
cancel.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a Sun whose disc shrinks, as it dims, by the amount this law requires.
fall.title: Eight orders of magnitude, and where the flat curves stop
fall.mini: Light on the ground relative to noon, on a log scale. Measured, it falls by a factor of 100 million from day to night. The flat-Earth curves level off far above that: a Sun a few thousand km up never gets far enough away.
fall.text: The light on level ground relative to noon, on a log scale where each gridline is a factor of ten, against ground distance. Measured, the day-to-night ratio is about 100 million; full sunlight is of order 100,000 lux and a clear moonless night of order 0.001 lux [1]. The flat curves, whatever the Sun's height, level off far above night, because a source at finite height never gets far away compared with itself. On a globe there is no curve past the day-night line at all: the direct beam is geometrically zero there, and every photon reaching you has been scattered down from the sunlit air above.
fall.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: night light levels matching the flat curves, a few times to a few hundred times dimmer than noon.
world.title: One instant, two geometries
world.labels: Globe|Plane, inverse-square light|Plane, fitted at 45° N
world.mini: The whole Earth at one instant, on a globe and on the flat-earth map lit two ways. With inverse-square light, night never falls on the plane. Tuned to be exact at 45° N, its day-night line is a circle; the real one is not.
world.text: The whole planet at the instant named above the text. On one side, a globe shaded by the Sun's altitude, with the three twilight thresholds; on the other, the same instant on the standard flat map, lit in the two ways a plane can be. With inverse-square light, from a lamp 5,000 km above the plane, it never gets dark: the dimmest point, at the map's 20,000 km rim, still receives 1/70 of noon, while a real night is about a hundred-millionth of daylight [2], which on this plane would need 2.3 million km, six times the distance to the Moon. The fitted version gives the flat model its best case: the light law is whatever puts the day-night edge exactly right at 45° N. Any brightness that decreases with distance from the point beneath the Sun has circles as its contours, so its boundary is a circle, whatever the law. The dashed teal curve is where sunset is really happening, from the published sunrise and sunset tables [1]: it is not a circle. The globe's twilight shading is schematic.
world.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: published sunrise and sunset times that fall on a circle around the point beneath the Sun.
meridian.title: Why some places get no night in June
meridian.mini: In the meridian plane the celestial pole stands at your latitude, and the Sun's daily circle tilts with it. The lowest point of that circle, at midnight, decides whether night comes at all. No distance enters.
meridian.text: Draw the plane of the meridian. The celestial pole stands at your latitude φ above the northern horizon, and the Sun's daily circle is tilted with it, at the Sun's declination δ from the equator. The Sun's altitude at local midnight, the lowest point of that circle, decides everything: if it never reaches −18°, there is no astronomical night at that place on that date, however long you wait. The formula contains no distance and no radius, only the latitude, the declination and the tilt; an independent implementation of it is published by a second institution [1]. The drawing is schematic.
meridian.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: full darkness at high latitudes in June, where the sphere's geometry forbids it.
duration.title: Twilight length against latitude
duration.mini: At midsummer, astronomical night disappears north of 48.6°, nautical night north of 54.6°, and civil night north of 60.6°: the white nights. Three sharp latitudes, from the Earth's tilt alone. A flat model has no answer.
duration.text: Twilight length against latitude at midsummer, June in the north and December in the south. Set the Sun's midnight altitude to −18° and the condition falls out: astronomical night disappears above latitude 90° − 18° − 23.44°, that is 48.6°. Nautical night goes at 54.6° and civil night, the genuine white nights, at 60.6°. Three sharp latitudes, predicted from the tilt of the Earth's axis and nothing else, each checkable in a published almanac [1], with an independent solar calculator [2], or by going outside in June. It is a yes-or-no test: at 48° astronomical night occurs in the third week of June, at 49° it does not. A Sun above a plane never crosses a horizon, and nothing in it produces a latitude past which twilight lasts all night.
duration.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: astronomical night in late June north of 49°, or twilight of the same length at every latitude.
shadow.title: The Earth's shadow, in the evening sky
shadow.mini: Ten minutes after sunset, look east: a dark blue-grey band lies along the horizon, a pink band above it. The dark band is the Earth's own shadow on the air. Its top rises as the Sun sinks. On a plane nothing could cast it.
shadow.text: On a clear evening, turn your back on the sunset about ten minutes after the Sun has gone. A dark blue-grey band lies along the eastern horizon, with a soft pink band above it, the Belt of Venus: sunlight reddened in the lower air and scattered back [1]. The dark band is the Earth's own shadow cast on the air, seen edge-on. It behaves as a shadow must: it sits opposite the Sun, and its top rises as the Sun sinks, its height set by the Sun's depression, until it fades out on thinning air. The drawing shows the eastern sky at three moments after sunset; the colours are indicative, the heights of the boundary are computed. The flat model predicts no edge at all, since nothing stands between the observer and the Sun to cast one.
shadow.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: no dark band opposite the setting Sun, or one that does not rise as the Sun sinks.
